title: Asthma attack first aid, repeat cycles
version: Cardiac and Respiratory Foundation NZ posters 'Asthma First Aid in School' (July 2026) and 'Asthma First Aid, adolescent and adult 12 years +' (July 2026); the Foundation's 'Asthma' web page and Health NZ's info.health.nz 'Mate huangō Asthma' page (no dates shown); Asthma Australia 'Asthma First Aid' Blue/Grey Reliever poster v13 (2026); Better Health Channel 'Asthma emergency first aid' (reviewed 12-11-2025); all read 19 Nov 2026
sourceNote: The Asthma and Respiratory Foundation NZ is now the Cardiac and Respiratory Foundation NZ: asthmafoundation.org.nz links redirect to cardiacandrespiratory.org.nz, and the old 'Asthma-First-Aid.pdf' no longer exists. Main source (A) is the Foundation's July 2026 'Asthma First Aid in School' poster, the only NZ poster that gives the full repeat cycle in numbers. Also copied: the Foundation's July 2026 poster for adolescents and adults 12 years + (B), the Foundation's 'Asthma' web page written for parents (C), Health NZ's info.health.nz asthma page (D), and as a separate Australian source Asthma Australia's 2026 blue/grey reliever poster (E) with the Better Health Channel (Victoria) page (E2) used to confirm its numbers. The sites block downloads here, so every line was read by a fetch tool asked to quote exact lines. Poster text comes out in a jumbled order, so which step some lines sit under is inferred, and Asthma Australia step numbers were put in front of the headings by hand. THE NUMBERS DIFFER, so the sources are kept under separate headings. NZ (A, C, D): 6 puffs one at a time through a spacer, 6 breaths per puff, wait 6 minutes, then 6 puffs every 6 minutes until help arrives; call 111. A and C say mild symptoms get 2 puffs and moderate or severe get 6; D says 6 puffs 'if you are not sure of the dose'. A says call an ambulance if not improving after 6 minutes, and dial 111 straight away if the child has severe asthma or is frightened; A also says 'you will not overdose the person'. D says if there is no improvement 'see a doctor immediately' and only calls 111 'in an emergency', which is weaker than A. B (12 years +) does not use the 6-minute cycle: it says 'Give ONE dose at a time of a RELIEVER inhaler', 'Repeat if necessary, up to 6 times', then if not improving dial 111 and keep using the reliever 'every few minutes'; with a spacer, 1 puff and 6 breaths per puff. B lists reliever examples including Symbicort, Vannair and DuoResp Spiromax (anti-inflammatory relievers), so one dose means different things for different inhalers; B gives no dose for each. Australia (E): 4 separate puffs, 4 breaths per puff from a spacer, wait 4 minutes, then 4 puffs every 4 minutes, dial triple zero (000); without a spacer, 1 puff with 1 slow deep breath. The extracted step 3 heading read 'WAIT 4 3 MINUTES' (the 3 is the step number graphic); the Better Health page confirms 'Wait 4 minutes'. Only E covers no reliever available (call 000 at once), not sure it is asthma, and known allergy with sudden breathing difficulty ('GIVE ADRENALINE FIRST (if available)'); none of the NZ sources mention adrenaline, anaphylaxis or what to do with no reliever. Asthma Australia's posters for other reliever types (dry powder 2 inhalations, Rapihaler 4 puffs, Fostair 2 puffs, 'Don't wait 4 minutes if symptoms are severe') were not copied. Healthify NZ's 'Asthma – first aid' page was read but not copied: it is run by a charitable trust, not Health NZ, and it gives inhaler-specific doses (for example 'up to 12 puffs daily' for Symbicort) that do not match the posters. Two images on the posters (layout, icons) could not be read. Dropping the poster PDFs into sources/ would make checking exact.
status: Reviewer: 4 instructions missed (incl. repeat puffs at 6 minutes) and 11 findings, all fixed. 56 of 56 quotes exact (web copy).
